analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to negotiate lower drug prices for Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices died in House committee without a markup or a single vote, despite bipartisan sponsorship from one Republican and 27 Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have deleted the current rule that forbids Medicare from negotiating drug prices, and instead required the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with drug manufacturers for all Medicare prescription drug plans. It would have preserved each plan's freedom to design its own formulary and let plans bargain for prices below whatever the government negotiated. The bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 35 million Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in prescription drug plans, who pay premiums and cost-sharing tied to drug prices. Medicare itself would also benefit, since lower negotiated prices reduce what taxpayers pay for the program. If prices came down, private plans could pass savings to enrollees as lower premiums and copays.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'noninterference' rule added when Medicare Part D was created, which bars the HHS Secretary from negotiating drug prices on behalf of Medicare.

Requires the Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, rebates, and other price concessions with pharmaceutical manufacturers for covered Part D drugs for enrollees in both standalone drug plans and Medicare Advantage drug plans.
Preserves beneficiaries' access rules: the Secretary cannot impose a particular formulary, and private plans remain free to negotiate prices below the government-negotiated price.
Adds semi-annual reports to Congress on the negotiations and the prices and discounts achieved, creating public accountability for the results.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, which would face a single large payer negotiating on behalf of the biggest drug market in the country rather than dealing with dozens of private plans one at a time. Generic manufacturers and pharmacy benefit middlemen could also see their margins squeezed if the negotiated benchmark tightened.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes negotiation without giving the Secretary the leverage of a required formulary or the power to refuse to cover a drug, so the savings it could actually produce depend entirely on how hard the government bargains; a negotiated price with no fallback may extract little from manufacturers.
The bill takes effect for plan year 2012, one year after introduction, leaving little time to stand up a negotiation apparatus before its first application date.

Good-faith opponents of Medicare price negotiation argued that private competition among Part D plans had already held prices down, and that a single government negotiator could reduce manufacturers' incentive to bring innovative drugs to market. The bill's drafters addressed the formulary concern but left the broader innovation debate unresolved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for seniors and taxpayers is potentially large, since drugs are a major share of Medicare spending and a single negotiator representing the largest buyer in the market has leverage no private plan can match. The design weakness is real: without formulary leverage, the bill relies on negotiation alone, so its savings could fall short of its promise. The main obstacle it faced was not its drafting but the fact that it was never allowed a committee vote or floor action at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to their health subcommittees, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 21, 2011 by Rep. Peter Welch (D-VT) together with Rep. Jo Ann Emerson (R-MO) and referred to two committees: Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means.
Within days it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health in each committee (June 22 and July 7, 2011), which is where the record of action ends.

The bill attracted 29 cosponsors, 27 Democrats and 2 Republicans, but no subcommittee, full committee, or House floor action ever followed, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept the existing legal ban on Medicare drug price negotiation for another two years. Private drug plans and pharmacy middlemen also kept their role as the pricing channel. Seniors and taxpayers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require Medicare to negotiate drug prices and recruited a bipartisan cosponsor.

for.name: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson
for.what_they_did: Joined Welch as an original cosponsor, giving the bill Republican sponsorship in the House.

for.name: 27 House Democrats and 2 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it received before it stalled.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sent it to their health subcommittees, and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed government negotiation of Medicare drug prices and defended the noninterference provision the bill would repeal.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic, 27 of 29 cosponsors, though a Republican chair of a House appropriations subcommittee, Jo Ann Emerson, signed on as an original cosponsor; the committee that buried it was controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill strips the statutory ban on Medicare negotiating prices, subjecting the industry's largest payer to a single government negotiator seeking discounts and rebates. The industry's interest in keeping the ban runs against seniors and taxpayers who pay Part D prices.

industries.industry: Private Medicare drug plans (PDP and MA-PD sponsors)
industries.note: Plans would have to accept the negotiated price as a ceiling for what they pay manufacturers, squeezing intermediaries' margins, but they keep formulary control and can negotiate even lower prices themselves, and lower input costs could support lower premiums for enrollees.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug-distribution middlemen
industries.note: A government-negotiated benchmark could compress the spread these intermediaries capture between manufacturer prices and plan payments, though the bill leaves their formulary and contracting role intact.
